source.title: Scaling Pre-Training to One Hundred Billion Data for Vision Language Models
source.authors: Xiao Wang; Ibrahim M. Alabdulmohsin; Daniel M. Salz; Zhe Li; Ke-Ran Rong; Xiao-Qi Zhai

record.file_problem: None noted; the paper and appendices are present. Some tables are flattened in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law evaluation to contrastively pretrained vision-language models and reports results as data and compute scale vary. It does not reproduce language-model held-out cross-entropy experiments.
record.gate_note: The study explicitly fits data-scaling laws for vision-language benchmark results, and reports downstream benchmark outcomes across data and compute scales. It does not measure language-model pretraining loss or test parameter/token compute-optimal allocation. It evaluates transfer to generative models, but does not fit a power law for that transfer. Many task-level and language-level results are omitted under the 60-row cap; cited results from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures downstream performance as vision-language pretraining data, model size and training compute vary, and fits scaling curves in this new modality. It bears on V5 and V6, and its dataset-dependent fitted exponents bear on the data-setup component of V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: scaling to 100B unique image-text pairs brings limited traditional Western benchmark gains, stronger cultural and low-resource-language benefits, and no consistent gains in generative-model transfer. The conclusion also emphasizes filtering's cultural-diversity costs and some reductions in performance disparity; it does not claim that scaling removes representation or association bias.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than autoregressive language-model pretraining measured by held-out cross-entropy, the study trains contrastive SigLIP vision-language models on image-text data and evaluates downstream vision-language tasks. It fits data-scaling laws for benchmark results, not the original language-model loss curves.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes differ by benchmark domain, dataset scale, compute budget, vision-model size, and whether the transferred vision component is frozen or unfrozen.
record.code_released: no; the paper says raw data, metadata files, and pipeline code are not released
record.peer_reviewed: 2026 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition—Findings Track (CVPRF), as stated in the supplied metadata
record.problems: The paper says joint scaling laws for model size and compute are computationally prohibitive at these data scales. Model sizes are restricted to ViT-H (approximately 600M parameters), and the authors note that inclusivity benchmarks cover limited measures and language/image samples. Raw data, metadata, and pipeline code are not released. Many task-level scaling results are given in large tables; only selected aggregates and compute-scaling comparisons are extracted here.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports more than 60 relevant task-level outcomes across Appendix B, Tables 8–9; Appendix E, Table 11; transfer Table 12; data-filtering Tables 13–14; per-language multilingual results in Appendix E; and compute-scaling Tables 16–19. Under the row cap, this record prioritizes selected compute-scaling metrics, transfer aggregates, and model-level aggregate Western, cultural, and low-resource-language results. Other per-task/per-language values, filtering comparisons, and fairness results are omitted.

untested.parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or unconstrained parameter/token/compute loss law.
No held-out validation of small-run forecasts against runs orders of magnitude larger; fitted infinite-compute limits are extrapolations without such validation.
No optimization of parameter and token counts across fixed compute budgets or fitted compute-optimal allocation powers.
No architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.

No demonstrated universal power-law form across modalities, fine-tuning or generative transfer; no reported fit-quality or forecasting validation establishing that the chosen form is uniquely adequate.
No relationship to language-model pretraining loss and no validated quantitative forecasts of larger-run downstream performance.

No controlled comparison of fitting algorithms, parameter counting or schedules; no compute-optimal split, explanation of disagreements between published language-model laws, or formal test of curve bending.

missing.what: Actual fitted scaling exponents and asymptotic limits. For H ImageNet, Table 8 reports exponents -0.36, -0.64, -0.52 and limits 26.7, 24.5, 23.3 for 1B, 10B, 100B datasets. H COCO I2T exponents are -0.21, -0.62, -0.47 and limits 44.6, 40.3, 40.6. These characterize training-progress fits within each dataset condition, not an exponent fitted solely across the three unique-data sizes. Although rows_left_out mentions omitted task outcomes, it does not explicitly declare omission of the fitted law parameters.

Suite-level significance tests for 10B versus 100B: Western benchmark improvements are non-significant, p=0.9; fitted asymptotic performance differences are also non-significant, p=0.09; cultural benchmark gains are significant, p=0.002. Endpoint rows do not capture these tests.

record.verdict_notes: Unique dataset size and training examples seen must be distinguished: the primary 1B/10B/100B comparisons all see 100B training examples, so smaller datasets are repeated. Diminishing gains alone do not challenge a power law with a nonzero asymptote. V5 support rests on the fitted curves, not on endpoint improvements or the transfer rows. V7 support is restricted to dataset-dependent fitted exponents and does not establish fitting-method sensitivity. Table 12's flattened column ordering conflicts with its header; Table 2 and its task-group averages support the transfer assignments used here.

versions.untested_parts: No language models or held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss are measured.
No test of whether fits on small runs predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

The study tests data scaling for image-text vision-language pretraining, but not whether fitted laws transfer to other modalities such as video or to repeated-data and fine-tuning regimes. It reports generative-model transfer results but does not fit scaling laws for that transfer.

Measures selected downstream classification, retrieval, and transfer outcomes under data and compute scaling; does not test downstream predictability from language-model pretraining loss or validate small-run forecasts against much larger runs.
Does not compare fitting methods or parameter-counting choices, nor test whether fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations change with setup.

relationships.condition: Fitted benchmark-error curves during contrastive vision-language training on fixed 1B, 10B and 100B datasets
relationships.reason: Based on Section 4.1 and Tables 8–9, missing from the rows: the authors fit scaling curves and report exponents and asymptotic limits in a vision-language regime; support is descriptive because fit quality is not reported.
relationships.display_finding: Benchmark-error scaling fits yield exponents and asymptotic limits, although fit quality is unreported.

relationships.condition: Substantial cultural and low-resource-language gains, particularly with larger models and sufficient training
relationships.reason: J10–J13, J15–J16, A10–A18 show improving downstream results; H low-resource error falls from 86.58 to 70.93 in A18.
relationships.display_finding: Downstream performance improved, including H low-resource-language error decreasing from 86.58 to 70.93.

relationships.condition: H ImageNet and COCO, increasing unique data from 1B to 10B or 100B with 100B examples seen
relationships.reason: J3–J4 and J7 show clear improvements over the 1B-data baseline, without establishing continued substantial gains beyond 10B.
relationships.display_finding: ImageNet and COCO improved over the 1B unique-data baseline, without establishing continued substantial gains beyond 10B unique examples.

relationships.condition: Small gains on Western aggregates and selected small-model cultural comparisons
relationships.reason: A1–A9 improve only modestly; A2 and A6 add just 0.03 and 0.05 error points of improvement beyond 10B unique pairs.
relationships.display_finding: Several comparisons improved only modestly, with two gaining just 0.03 and 0.05 error points beyond 10B unique pairs.

relationships.condition: Low training budget or non-monotonic task-specific data scaling
relationships.reason: Corrected J1–J2 and J5–J6 give small gains, J9 gains 0.4 points, and J8 and J14 fall relative to the intermediate data scale.
relationships.display_finding: Gains were small under low training budgets, including a 0.4-point improvement, while two task-specific results declined relative to the intermediate data scale.

relationships.condition: Western benchmark suite, 10B to 100B unique pairs at matched training compute
relationships.reason: Section 4.1 explicitly reports no significant improvement, p=0.9; this suite-level test is missing from the rows and challenges reliable improvement in this interval.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing unique pairs from 10B to 100B at matched training compute produced no significant benchmark improvement, with p=0.9.

relationships.condition: PaliGemma transfer from 1B to 10B unique-pair vision pretraining, frozen and unfrozen
relationships.reason: TR1 and TR3 averages fall from 73.6 to 72.7 and 75.1 to 73.7; the authors treat the drops as noise, so they challenge consistent gains rather than establish reliable deterioration.
relationships.display_finding: Frozen and unfrozen transfer averages fell from 73.6 to 72.7 and 75.1 to 73.7, respectively, although the authors interpreted these decreases as noise.

relationships.condition: PaliGemma transfer from 1B to 100B unique-pair vision pretraining, frozen and unfrozen
relationships.reason: TR2 and TR4 improve by only 0.3 and 0.2 points, and Section 4.5 reports no consistent task-level gains.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing vision pretraining from 1B to 100B unique pairs yielded only 0.3- and 0.2-point gains, without consistent task-level improvements.

relationships.condition: Changing the unique pretraining dataset while fitting training-progress curves
relationships.reason: Based on Table 8, missing from the rows: H COCO I2T fitted exponents are -0.21, -0.62 and -0.47 for 1B, 10B and 100B datasets, showing setup-dependent fitted values.
relationships.display_finding: H COCO I2T training-progress exponents were −0.21, −0.62, and −0.47 for unique datasets of 1B, 10B, and 100B, respectively.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Image-text vision-language pretraining, tested data scales and benchmark settings
reader_labels.reason: The authors fit data-scaling laws for benchmark combinations and report data-scale improvements in cultural and low-resource-language aggregates; relevant outcomes are in J1–J16 and A7–A18.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Western-centric benchmarks and transfer to generative models
reader_labels.reason: Western aggregate changes are small, some compute-table values are non-monotonic, and generative-transfer averages do not improve consistently; this is not evidence for a universal law across regimes.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Cultural-diversity benchmarks and low-resource multilingual retrieval
reader_labels.reason: The reported aggregate errors fall with data scale in these settings, including the H/14 low-resource-language average from 86.58 to 70.93; see J9–J16 and A7–A18.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Western aggregate improvements are described as marginal, some individual compute/data comparisons are non-monotonic, and the transfer averages show no consistent gains.
